title: Array With Saved Versions
statement:
Build an array of integers that can save versions of itself, like a tiny undo history.

  • VersionedArray(length) creates an array of length slots, all holding 0.
  • set(index, val) writes val into slot index of the live array.
  • snap() saves the current contents as a new version and returns its id. Ids start at 0 and go up by one per call.
  • get(index, snapId) returns what slot index held at the moment version snapId was saved. snapId is always an id that snap() has already returned.

Copying the whole array on every snap() is too slow and too big when the array is long and most slots never change. Only store what changed.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first one creates the array. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Version 0 saw slot 1 = 7. Writing 9 afterwards changes the live array and version 1, not version 0. Slot 2 was never written, so it reads 0.
Only the last write before a snap counts. Versions 1 and 2 changed nothing, so slot 0 in version 2 still holds the 5 written before version 0.

constraints: 0 ≤ snapId < number of snap() calls so far
hints: Most slots never change between two versions. What is the smallest thing you could record per slot?
For each slot, keep a list of (version id, value) pairs, added only when the slot is written. The list is sorted by version id for free, because ids only grow.
To answer get(index, snapId), binary-search that slot's list for the last entry whose version id is ≤ snapId. If there is none, the answer is 0.

explain.intuition:
Think of a version-control system: it does not store a full copy of the repo per commit, only the changes. Here, each slot keeps its own little history: "from version v onward, I hold value x". A write during the current, not-yet-saved version just overwrites that version's entry, so each slot gets at most one entry per version.

Because version ids only increase, each history list is sorted by id without any extra work. Reading slot i at version s means finding the last change made at or before s, which is a binary search: "the rightmost entry with id ≤ s".
steps: Keep current = 0, the id the next snap() will return, and for every slot a list of [id, value] pairs.
set(i, v): if slot i's last entry has id current, overwrite its value; otherwise append [current, v].
snap(): return current and then add one to it.
get(i, s): binary-search slot i's list for the rightmost entry with id ≤ s. Return its value, or 0 if every entry is newer (or the list is empty).
pitfalls: Copying the whole array in snap(). With 50 000 slots and 50 000 snaps, that is 2.5 billion copies.
Searching for an exact id match. Version 2 may contain no change to slot i at all; you need the latest change at or before it.
Recording a write under the id that snap() just returned. A write after snap() belongs to the next version, not the saved one.

complexity.time: O(1) for set and snap, O(log s) for get

solutions.title: Copy everything on snap
solutions.idea: Keep the live array and push a full copy of it on every snap. Correct, but each snap costs O(length).
solutions.time: O(length) per snap, O(1) for get and set

solutions.title: Per-slot change history and binary search
solutions.idea: Each slot stores (version, value) pairs only when written. A read finds the last change at or before the requested version.
solutions.time: O(1) for set and snap, O(log s) for get

followups: Add diff(a, b), returning which slots differ between two versions. What would you store to make it fast?
How does this compare to the structural sharing used by immutable data libraries such as Immer?
